content.text: Source: the supplied Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 — RH134 book. I’ll follow the chapter’s order and explain it in simple English, with commands and practical examples.
This chapter teaches you two main skills:
Adjust tuning profiles — choose settings that suit what a computer is doing.
Influence process scheduling — give a process more or less priority when competing for CPU time.

Imagine your computer is a kitchen. The CPU is the chef, and running programs are the orders waiting to be prepared. Tuning helps organize the kitchen; process scheduling helps decide which orders receive attention first.
1.1 What is system tuning?
Main idea: Adjust system settings to better suit the computer’s workload.
Simple explanation: A server used for virtual machines may need different settings from a desktop computer. Red Hat provides tuning profiles so you do not need to adjust every setting manually.
The tuned service applies these settings using predefined profiles.
Example:
systemctl status tuned
What each part means:
systemctl manages and checks services.
status displays the service’s current state.
tuned is the service that applies tuning settings.
Remember: tuned helps configure system performance for a particular workload.
1.2 Static tuning vs dynamic tuning
Main idea: Tuning settings can be applied in two ways.
Static tuning: Settings are applied when the service starts or when a profile changes. They do not keep changing as activity changes.
Dynamic tuning: The system monitors activity and adjusts settings as workload changes.
Analogy: Static tuning is setting a fan to one speed. Dynamic tuning is a fan that automatically speeds up when the room gets hot and slows down when it cools.
Remember: Static means settings stay as configured; dynamic means settings can adapt to changing activity.
1.3 Check whether tuned is installed and running
Example:
yum list tuned
systemctl is-enabled tuned
systemctl is-active tuned
What each part means:
yum list tuned checks the package information and whether the package is installed.
systemctl is-enabled tuned checks whether the service is configured to start automatically at boot.
systemctl is-active tuned checks whether the service is running now.
Possible results include enabled and active. They mean different things: a service can be enabled for startup but not currently running.
Remember: Enabled means set to start automatically; active means running now.
1.4 View and change tuning profiles
Main idea: tuned-adm lets you view, select, and check tuning profiles.
Important commands:
tuned-adm list
tuned-adm active
tuned-adm recommend
sudo tuned-adm profile balanced
tuned-adm profile_info
What each part means:
list — shows available profiles.
active — shows the profile currently in use.
recommend — suggests a profile for the system.
profile balanced — switches to the balanced profile.
profile_info — displays information about the active profile.
sudo — runs the command with administrator privileges.
The book also explains turning tuning off:
sudo tuned-adm off
This deactivates tuning managed by tuned.
1.5 Know the common profiles
Profile
Purpose
balanced
Compromise between power saving and performance
powersave
Save power
throughput-performance
Focus on processing more work
latency-performance
Focus on low delay
network-latency
Focus on low network delay
network-throughput
Focus on network data transfer
desktop
Improve response for interactive desktop applications
virtual-guest
Tune a virtual machine
virtual-host
Tune a host running virtual machines
oracle
Optimize for Oracle database workloads
Remember: Choose the profile for the system’s purpose, not simply because its name sounds faster.
1.6 Manage profiles through the Web Console
The book also shows profile management through the RHEL Web Console:
Log in with privileges that allow administrative changes.
Open System.
Find Performance Profile.
Select the profile you need.
Return to the System page and verify the active profile.
Remember: You can manage profiles from the command line or through the Web Console.
2.1 What is process scheduling?
Main idea: The operating system decides which processes receive CPU time.
A process is a running program. When many processes need the CPU, Linux schedules their work so they can make progress.
The nice value influences a process’s scheduling priority. In Linux, values normally range from -20 to 19:
-20: higher scheduling priority.
0: normal nice value.
19: lower scheduling priority.
Analogy: Imagine several people waiting for a service. A process with a lower nice value generally gets more favorable CPU scheduling than one with a higher nice value.
Remember: Lower nice value = higher priority; higher nice value = lower priority. This influences scheduling—it does not guarantee a fixed amount of CPU time.
2.2 Start a command with a nice value
Use nice when starting a new process.
Example:
nice -n 10 sha1sum /dev/zero
What each part means:
nice — starts a command with a selected nice value.
-n 10 — requests nice value 10.
sha1sum — calculates a checksum.
/dev/zero — supplies a continuous stream of zero bytes.
This example is intended to demonstrate scheduling; sha1sum /dev/zero keeps processing data, so do not run it casually on your everyday system. The book uses it in a controlled lab.
Remember: nice sets the nice value when launching a command.
2.3 Find processes and their CPU usage
The book uses ps to inspect running processes.
ps aux --sort=pcpu
What each part means:
ps — displays process information.
a and u — request a broad process listing with user-oriented details.
x — includes processes that are not attached to a terminal.
--sort=pcpu — sorts the results by CPU usage.
To display selected details for particular processes, the book also uses:
ps -o pid,pcpu,nice,comm
This displays the process ID (pid), CPU usage (pcpu), nice value (nice), and command name (comm).
Remember: Inspect processes first so you know which process you want to adjust.
2.4 Change the nice value of a running process
Use renice when the process is already running.
renice -n 10 3521
What each part means:
renice — changes the nice value of an existing process.
-n 10 — sets the requested nice value to 10.
3521 — example process ID (PID). Use the actual PID on your system.
To adjust multiple processes, the book demonstrates:
sudo renice -n 10 2967 2983
Here, 2967 and 2983 are example PIDs from the book’s lab, not values to copy blindly.

Important permission rule: Ordinary users can generally make a process less favorable by increasing its nice value. Lowering the nice value to give it higher priority usually requires administrator privileges.
Remember the difference:
nice — starts a command with a nice value.
renice — changes the nice value of a running process.
2.5 Guided exercise: Observe scheduling changes
The book’s guided exercise creates test processes and changes their nice values so you can observe scheduling behavior.
The important workflow is:
Check how many CPU cores are available.
Start test processes in the background in the controlled lab.
Use ps to inspect their CPU usage and nice values.
Use renice to adjust their nice values.
Observe the changes and finish the exercise.
For example, the book checks CPU core count with:
grep -c '^processor' /proc/cpuinfo
grep searches text.
-c counts matching lines.
^processor matches lines beginning with processor.
/proc/cpuinfo contains information about the system’s CPUs.
The book also uses top to monitor running processes. Inside top, pressing r lets you change a process’s nice value.
Safety note: The book’s lab commands are designed for its training environment. Avoid creating CPU-intensive test processes on your normal computer unless you know how to stop them.
The lab combines both major skills.
Task 1 — Change a tuning profile
On the lab server, the book selects the balanced profile:
sudo tuned-adm profile balanced
Then verify the profile:
sudo tuned-adm profile_info
Task 2 — Lower the scheduling priority of CPU-heavy processes
First, inspect CPU usage:
ps aux --sort=pcpu
Identify the relevant process IDs, then inspect their nice values:
ps -o pid,pcpu,nice,comm
Finally, use renice with the actual PIDs you identified.
What the lab is teaching: Do not guess which processes need adjustment. Inspect the system, make a targeted change, and verify the result.
1. Tune the whole system
Use tuned-adm to select settings suited to the computer’s workload.
2. Find processes that need attention
Use ps or top to inspect processes and their CPU usage.
3. Adjust an individual process
Use nice when starting a command and renice to change a running process.
Think of it this way: a tuning profile adjusts the system for its overall job; nice values influence how individual processes compete for CPU time.

One important detail for your practice: this textbook is for RHEL 8. Your RHEL 10 system may have a different set of available tuning profiles, so check tuned-adm list on your own machine rather than assuming every profile in the book is present.
1. Which command lists the available tuning profiles?
ps aux
tuned-adm list
renice -n 10
2. You want to change the nice value of a process that is already running. Which command should you use?
nice
renice
tuned-adm active
3. Which nice value normally gives a process higher scheduling priority?
Try again
Chapter 3 summary: Learn the tuned profiles, understand how Linux schedules processes, inspect CPU usage with ps or top, and use nice and renice appropriately.
